clue.text: Bold being in water off Cowes

parts.note: being in somewhere is simply to be in it
the Solent is the strait between the Isle of Wight, where Cowes stands, and the English mainland

explanation.surface: A boat or swimmer bobbing in the sea off the yachting town of Cowes.
explanation.walkthrough: Cowes is a sailing town on the Isle of Wight; the water it faces is the Solent.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe cheeky, brazen behaviour that shows no respect.

clue.text: I'd put up with anxiety and trouble

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting something up turns its letters so they read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written, I and D
stress is strain or anxiety

explanation.surface: Someone saying they have tolerated worry and difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' looks like 'tolerated', but in this down clue it turns ID upwards into DI.
explanation.definitionFit: Distress as a verb means to upset or worry someone, a synonym of trouble.

clue.text: Corps re-shuffled at No 10- some stars emerge

indicators.note: a reshuffle rearranges posts, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder
the figures 1 and 0 are read as the letters I and O

explanation.surface: A cabinet reshuffle at Number 10 Downing Street brings new stars out.
explanation.walkthrough: No 10 is the Prime Minister's residence in London, but here 10 just looks like the letters IO.
explanation.definitionFit: Scorpio is a zodiac constellation, a group of stars.

clue.text: Unstable atom in aluminium can blow up

indicators.note: one piece is placed in the middle of the other

parts.note: Al is the chemical symbol for aluminium

indicators.note: something unstable falls apart, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A warning that an unstable atom inside an aluminium can might explode.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can blow up' reads as a threat about the can, but 'can' belongs to the definition, not to the container signal 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: Amatol is a high explosive, something able to detonate.

parts.note: cave is Latin for beware, used as a schoolboy warning
RN is the Royal Navy, the sailors

explanation.surface: A warning to watch out for seamen lurking in a cave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cave!' (Latin 'beware') was the old British schoolboy call that a teacher was coming.
explanation.definitionFit: A cavern is a large cave, and a grotto is a small picturesque cave.

clue.text: Pair of drawers having only leg that makes an impression

definitions.text: Pair of drawers having only leg that makes an impression

parts.words: Pair of drawers having only leg that makes an impression
parts.note: drawers here are things that draw: an instrument with two legs, only one of which marks the paper

explanation.surface: Underwear with a single leg that leaves a mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pair of drawers' suggests underwear; it is a two-legged drawing instrument where only the pencil leg leaves a line.
explanation.definitionFit: The instrument for drawing circles has a point on one leg and a pencil on the other, and only the pencil marks.

clue.text: Kit kept car in Gateshead in wrong position? What did he get?

indicators.note: letters in the wrong position must be rearranged into the right order

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder
read as Gate's head, the first letter of gate

explanation.surface: Kit left the car parked in the wrong spot in Gateshead, so what penalty followed?
explanation.walkthrough: Gateshead is a town in north-east England; split as 'Gate's head' it gives G. 'in wrong position' signals the anagram and also describes the badly parked car.
explanation.definitionFit: A driver who leaves a car in the wrong place is given a fine notice for it.

parts.note: secret means hidden from others
a service is a supply of something, as in a bus service

explanation.surface: A covert supply line run for spies.
explanation.definitionFit: The intelligence service is the organisation employing spies, so it stands for its agents.

parts.note: in rugby a try is scored by touching the ball down
out means ruled out, not permitted

explanation.surface: A disallowed touchdown in a rugby Test match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Test' looks like a rugby international, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tryout is a trial run to see how something performs.

clue.text: Cut back of Conservative leader, her rent under review

indicators.note: being reviewed and reworked, so these letters are rearranged
the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A Tory leader's rent is being reviewed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut back' sounds like a description of the leader, but it is the definition. C plus HERRENT, rearranged by 'under review'.
explanation.definitionFit: To retrench is to reduce spending, to economise.

clue.text: Brief last thoughts on a rake?

definitions.meaning: ..., short for rest in peace, is the final wish on a gravestone
an old word for a dissolute man, a libertine

explanation.surface: A short epitaph carved for a dead libertine.
explanation.definitionFit: The abbreviation on tombstones is a brief farewell, and a rip is an old word for a debauched rogue.

parts.note: a bid in card games such as solo whist where the bidder undertakes to win no tricks at all

explanation.surface: An honest statement promising there is no deceit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No tricks' sounds like 'no deception'; in cards it means no tricks won.
explanation.definitionFit: In solo whist this call commits the player to losing every trick.

parts.note: to slander is to defame someone with false spoken words

explanation.surface: Someone confessing to smearing a person from Crete.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'perhaps' marks a Cretan as one example: Crete is an island.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Crete lives on an island, so is one example of an island-dweller.

explanation.surface: A measurement of one foot to the rear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' looks like a reversal signal, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Aft is the nautical word for towards the stern, the back of a ship.

clue.text: For example, "I"' most in use in it

definitions.text: For example, "I"' most in use in it

indicators.note: letters put to use are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: Self-centred talk is where the word I gets used most.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted I is the first-person pronoun, and 'in use' is the anagram signal; read whole, the clue also describes the answer, so it is an all-in-one.
explanation.definitionFit: Self-obsession shows in constant talk about oneself, using the first person most.

parts.note: the Roman numeral I is one
an MP, Member of Parliament, makes laws

explanation.surface: A single lawmaker tackling a tricky question.
explanation.walkthrough: 'issue' looks like a problem, but it means offspring: a naughty child.
explanation.definitionFit: Issue means children, and a mischievous little rascal is a troublesome child.

parts.note: colonel sounds like kernel, the edible core that sits inside a shell, and a crazy person is a case

explanation.surface: Rumour has it that the army colonel is mad.
explanation.walkthrough: Colonel and kernel sound the same; a kernel is a nut, and someone barmy is a nut or a case. Barmy is British slang for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: A crazy person is called a nut, so the word for a lunatic fits.

indicators.note: blenders mix things up, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: The final firm blending many teas.
explanation.definitionFit: Ultimate means final, coming at the end.

definitions.meaning: the bringing of something into being
Haydn's oratorio of 1798 sets the Genesis story of the world's making

explanation.surface: A turn in the music within one of Haydn's oratorios.
explanation.definitionFit: Bringing something into existence is a development, and Haydn's famous oratorio is The Creation.

parts.note: an owl is a thing that hoots, and slang for noses is the same word

explanation.surface: An exclamation about owls' beaks.
explanation.walkthrough: Owls hoot, so they are things that hoot; British slang also calls noses by that name.
explanation.definitionFit: Owls make hooting calls, and big noses are slangily called by the same word.

clue.text: Awkwardly, I pin folio endlessly-one in manila, say

indicators.note: done awkwardly, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

indicators.note: without its end, so the word loses its last letter

explanation.surface: Clumsily pinning a folio of papers in an office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' cuts the final O of FOLIO to FOLI, and 'Awkwardly' rearranges it with IPIN. Manila is the capital of the Philippines.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the Philippines, whose capital is Manila, is an example.

parts.note: Oberon's greeting to the fairy queen in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, with its opening words missing

explanation.surface: A line from A Midsummer Night's Dream with a gap.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing words of Oberon's line mean an unlucky or unwelcome meeting.

indicators.note: what is heard is said aloud, so this signals a word of the same sound

parts.note: said in jest is said not seriously, as a joke

explanation.surface: Eating, but only as a joke.
explanation.walkthrough: IN JEST and the answer sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: To take food or drink into the body is to swallow and consume it.

clue.text: He is included in right speculation

indicators.note: one piece is put inside another

parts.note: Tory means politically right-wing, of the Conservative Party
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man is said to be part of right-wing guesswork.
explanation.walkthrough: TORY is a member of the British Conservative Party, the political right.
explanation.definitionFit: A theory is a supposition, an idea not yet proven.

indicators.note: some of the word means only part of its letters are taken

explanation.surface: Undressing as part of a magic ritual.
explanation.definitionFit: Obi, also obeah, is a West Indian form of sorcery.

clue.text: Heavenly clue put up by glazier

parts.note: sky refers to the heavens above
a light is something that sheds light on a puzzle, a hint

explanation.surface: A clue from above offered by a glass-fitter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' is not a reversal: the glazier puts the window in a roof.
explanation.definitionFit: A glass window set into a roof is installed by a window fitter.

indicators.note: spread around, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Instructions to spread a tar mixture into a mould.
explanation.definitionFit: A matrix is a cast or die in which something is shaped.

clue.text: True over-rate's affected (not for the keeper, necessarily)

indicators.note: affected means altered, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Cricket talk about a bowling side's over-rate and the wicketkeeper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeper' suggests the cricket wicketkeeper; in fact valuables found in Britain are not always kept by the finder. An over-rate is how fast a cricket team bowls its overs.
explanation.definitionFit: Hidden valuables found buried may be claimed by the Crown rather than the person who finds them.
